mainEntity.name: How much does a Mercedes Benz E Class E63 AMG engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: A Mercedes Benz E Class E63 AMG engine replacement typically costs £4,500-£12,000+ supply-only, depending on the engine code. M156 complete used engines start from £4,100, M157 rebuilt units from £6,995, and M156 replacement motors average £10,149-£11,744. Specialist fitting adds £1,000-£2,000. M156 used: £4,100-£6,000; rebuilt: £9,000-£12,000. M157 used: £3,570-£5,000; rebuilt: £6,995-£9,500. M177 used: £7,000-£10,000; rebuilt: £11,000-£15,000.

mainEntity.name: What are the common problems with the Mercedes E63 AMG M156 engine?

acceptedAnswer.text: The M156 6.2L V8 in the E63 AMG is most notorious for head bolt failure. Early engines use bolts with insufficient material strength that can break, allowing coolant to leak into the combustion chamber. Engines with serial numbers before 60658 are affected. Camshaft adjuster wear and lifter tick are also reported. Head bolt failure can hydrolock the engine - catastrophic and expensive. Preventative head bolt replacement is strongly recommended on affected cars. A broken bolt repair can cost £5,500-£8,000 at a specialist.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine in a Mercedes E63 AMG?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes - if the car is otherwise sound. A used E63 AMG typically commands £9,000-£60,000+ depending on generation and mileage. A rebuilt M156 engine with warranty costs £9,000-£12,000, which is often justified relative to the vehicle's value. W211/W212 E63 AMG values: £9,000-£35,000. W213 E63 AMG values: £35,000-£60,000+. A rebuilt engine with 12-month warranty costs less than depreciation on a newer car. If the car has structural damage or transmission failure, evaluate replacing the whole vehicle instead.

mainEntity.name: How long does a Mercedes E63 AMG engine last?

acceptedAnswer.text: With proper maintenance and regular oil changes, E63 AMG engines can reach 100,000-150,000 miles. The M156 requires preventative head bolt replacement; the M157 is generally robust but needs camshaft adjuster attention; the M177 requires careful monitoring for bore scoring. M156: 100,000+ miles with head bolt upgrade. M157: 120,000+ miles with regular maintenance. M177: 100,000+ miles with careful monitoring. Regular oil analysis is recommended for all AMG V8s.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between the E63 AMG M156, M157 and M177 engines?

acceptedAnswer.text: The E63 AMG has used three V8 engines across its lifetime. The M156 (2006-2011) is a 6.2L naturally aspirated V8 producing 514-518hp. The M157 (2011-2016) is a 5.5L twin-turbo V8 producing 525-585hp. The M177 (2016-present) is a 4.0L twin-turbo V8 with hot-vee design producing 571-612hp. M156: naturally aspirated, high-revving, head bolt concerns. M157: twin-turbo, impressive reliability relative to output. M177: hot-vee twin-turbo, most powerful, bore scoring risk.

mainEntity.name: Does the Mercedes E63 AMG have a timing chain or belt?

acceptedAnswer.text: All E63 AMG engines use timing chains, not belts. Timing chain and tensioner wear is a known concern on higher-mileage M157 units. Cold-start rattle is the primary warning sign. M156: timing chain and camshaft adjuster wear possible. M157: timing chain stretch and camshaft adjuster wear reported. M177: timing chain inspection recommended from ~80,000 miles. Regular oil changes (every 10,000 miles) are critical for timing chain longevity.

historyTimeline.h2: Mercedes Benz E Class E63 AMG - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The E63 AMG arrived in 2006 as the flagship performance variant of the W211 E-Class, replacing the supercharged E55 AMG. It introduced the hand-built M156 6.2L naturally aspirated V8 - the first engine developed entirely in-house by AMG. Over three generations, the E63 has evolved through naturally aspirated, twin-turbo V8 and electrified powertrains, each pushing the boundaries of executive saloon performance.

milestones.description: M156 6.2L naturally aspirated V8, 514hp, introduced in W211 E63 AMG
W212 E63 AMG launched with M156 6.2L V8, 518hp
M157 5.5L twin-turbo V8 replaces M156 in W212, 525hp (557hp with Performance Pack)
M157 5.5L twin-turbo V8, 585hp, in W212 E63 AMG S 4MATIC
M177 4.0L twin-turbo V8 with hot-vee design, 571hp, debuts in W213 E63

commonProblems.h3: The Mercedes Benz E Class E63 AMG's hand-built V8 engines deliver extraordinary performance, but each generation carries its own well-documented weaknesses. The M156's head bolt failure, the M157's camshaft adjuster wear, and the M177's cylinder bore scoring all demand specialist attention. Rebuilt E63 AMG engines through EnginesMarket include upgraded components addressing the original failure point, plus a minimum 12-month unlimited-mileage warranty.

problems.h4: M156 Head Bolt Failure - The Achilles Heel of the 6.2L E63 AMG
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes Benz E Class E63 AMG (M156, W211 2006-2009; W212 2009-2011)
problems.rootCause: Early M156 engines use cylinder head bolts with insufficient material strength. Over time, the bolts can break, allowing coolant to enter the combustion chamber. A broken bolt can hydrolock the engine. Engines with serial numbers before 60658 are affected.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replacement of all head bolts with updated steel items, head gaskets, coolant flush
repairOptions.longevity: Must be done pre-failure; essential preventative work on affected cars

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Removal of broken bolts, head gasket replacement, cylinder head inspection
repairOptions.longevity: If bolts have broken but engine not hydrolocked

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit of rebuilt M156 with upgraded head bolts
repairOptions.longevity: If coolant has entered cylinders or engine is hydrolocked

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A used W211/W212 E63 AMG typically ranges from £9,000-£25,000. Preventative head bolt replacement (£2,500-£3,800 at a specialist) is excellent value relative to vehicle value. If failure has occurred and the engine requires full replacement, evaluate whether the repair cost approaches the vehicle's value - especially on higher-mileage examples.
problems.recommendation: If you own a pre-2011 E63 AMG that has NOT yet suffered head bolt failure, preventative replacement at an AMG specialist is essential - it is the single best value modification you can make. Once coolant has entered a cylinder, engine replacement is the only safe outcome. Never buy a used M156 E63 AMG without documented head bolt upgrade.
problems.cta: -> Compare rebuilt M156 Mercedes Benz E Class E63 AMG engine prices

problems.h4: M157 Camshaft Adjuster Wear - The 5.5L Twin-Turbo Weakness
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes Benz E Class E63 AMG (M157, W212 2011-2016)
problems.rootCause: Camshaft adjusters can wear, causing rattle on startup and eventual loss of timing accuracy. The issue is exacerbated by extended oil change intervals and high-performance driving.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replacement of camshaft adjusters, timing chain, and tensioner
repairOptions.longevity: If caught early with cold-start rattle

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Adjusters, chain, plus replacement of damaged lifters and valves
repairOptions.longevity: If timing has jumped and valves are damaged

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit of rebuilt M157 with upgraded components

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A W212 E63 AMG typically ranges from £15,000-£35,000. Camshaft adjuster replacement (£1,400-£2,200 at a specialist) is cost-effective on vehicles in this value bracket. Full engine replacement is justified if the car is otherwise sound.
problems.recommendation: Cold-start rattle on an M157 E63 AMG should not be ignored - it is the primary warning sign of camshaft adjuster wear. Address it preventatively at a specialist. If the engine has already jumped timing, a full rebuild or replacement is typically required.
problems.cta: -> Compare rebuilt M157 Mercedes Benz E Class E63 AMG engine prices

problems.h4: M177 Cylinder Bore Scoring - The 4.0L Hot-Vee Challenge
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes Benz E Class E63 AMG (M177, W213 2016-present)
problems.rootCause: Cylinder bore scoring can occur, particularly in higher-mileage examples. If a piston fails, the bore is typically damaged, making repair uneconomical.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Borescope inspection, compression test, oil analysis
Supply & fit of rebuilt M177 with upgraded pistons and liners
Supply & fit of used M177 from salvage
repairOptions.longevity: Lower-cost alternative; original design risk remains

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A W213 E63 AMG typically ranges from £35,000-£60,000+. Given the high vehicle value, engine replacement (£11,000-£15,000) is almost always justified relative to the car's worth.
problems.recommendation: Regular oil analysis and borescope inspections are recommended for high-mileage M177 E63 AMGs. If bore scoring is confirmed, a rebuilt engine with upgraded pistons and liners is the safest long-term solution - avoid used engines that carry the same design risk.
